notes.title: Dev Update – Optimization, Mocap & Darren’s Debut!
notes.content:
[p]We’re back with another development update from [b]Project Enceladus[/b]. This one dives a bit deeper into the techy side of things, so if you're into performance tricks, custom tools, and animation workflows — this is for you![/p][p][/p][h3][b]Performance Upgrades – Custom Data Layers & HISM[/b][/h3][p]As our levels grow larger and more complex, performance becomes a bigger concern — especially in a puzzle-platformer where flow and timing are everything.[/p][p]That’s why we built our own [b]Data Layer system in C++[/b]. Unlike Unreal’s World Partition system, this gives us more precise control:[/p][list][*][p]Load/unload actor groups using tags[/p][/*][*][p]Spread the work over frames with FTSTicker[/p][/*][*][p]Keep GPU usage stable and predictable[/p][/*][/list][p]It’s lightweight, custom-fit, and perfect for our level design needs.[/p][p]We also implemented [b]Hierarchical Instanced Static Meshes (HISM)[/b] in our new [b]Hangar level[/b] — a massive open space filled with detailed assets.[/p][p]Let’s just say:[/p][list][*][p]Before HISM? Our GPU cried.[/p][/*][*][p]After HISM? Silky smooth.[/p][/*][/list][p]We're now updating earlier levels to benefit from the same optimization.[/p][p][/p][hr][/hr][p][/p][h3][b]Mocap, but Make It Indie – Using Meta Quest for Hand Animation[/b][/h3][p]To bring our main character [b]Darren[/b] to life, we needed fluid, believable hand animation — without a full mocap studio.[/p][p]So we built our own [b]VR-based mocap workflow[/b] using a [b]Meta Quest headset[/b], directly inside [b]Unreal Engine 5[/b].[/p][p]The Setup:[/p][list][*][p]Meta Quest VR headset[/p][/*][*][p]Full-body IK system[/p][/*][*][p]Custom Blueprint + code logic[/p][/*][*][p]In-editor capture tools[/p][/*][*][p]Clean-up and polish directly in Unreal[/p][/*][*][p]Exported animations used in gameplay[/p][/*][/list][p]It's quick, scalable, and fits our indie toolkit perfectly.[/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45507777/2dd4b2ffa47690340609fd1cd56cea65d5c2acae.png"][/img][/p][hr][/hr][p][/p][h3][b]Meet Darren – Our Metahuman Protagonist[/b][/h3][p]Darren, our lead character, now has a finalized [b]Metahuman model[/b] — and it’s looking sharp.[/p][p]Since storytelling and expression are central to the game, we’re using the new [b]Metahuman Animator plugin in UE 5.6[/b] to drive facial performance and emotion in real time.[/p][p]It’s still early days, but we’re excited about how much nuance we can capture. We’ll share facial animation tests soon![/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45507777/bf5f16cf5490936ca6b208e7e0487a5a3d7e561f.png"][/img][/p][p][/p][hr][/hr][p][/p][h3][b]What We’re Working on Next:[/b][/h3][list][*][p]Facial mocap testing and refinement[/p][/*][*][p]Finalize animations, extend the State Machine of Darren[/p][/*][*][p]Wrapping up Level 5 of Chapter I[/p][/*][/list][p][/p][hr][/hr][p][/p][p]Thanks for reading, and for being part of this journey![/p][p][/p][p][b]– The Dev Team[/b]
[/p]

notes.title: Why Sci-Fi? Why Puzzles? Why Thriller? Why this style?
notes.content:
[p]As we get deeper into development on [b]Project Enceladus[/b], we wanted to take a step back and share something a bit more personal:
[b]Why this game? Why this genre mix? Why this tone?[/b][/p][p][/p][p]The answer is layered. Like the game itself.[/p][p][/p][h3]Why Sci-Fi?[/h3][p][/p][p]For many of us on the team, sci-fi wasn’t just a genre we liked — it’s something that shaped how we see storytelling and creativity.
We grew up watching, playing, and reading science fiction that wasn’t about laser guns or space battles… but about ideas.[/p][p]Stories that asked uncomfortable questions:
[i]What happens when technology outpaces humanity’s ethics?[/i]
[i]How far would we push science in the name of survival?[/i]
[i]Can progress and morality coexist?[/i][/p][p]Games like [b]SOMA[/b], movies like [b]Arrival[/b], or even classics like [b]2001: A Space Odyssey[/b] showed us how deeply sci-fi can tap into human emotion — and into fear.
Not fear of monsters… but fear of isolation, of the unknown, and of our own decisions.[/p][p][/p][h3]Why Puzzle-Platformer?[/h3][p][/p][p]We’ve always loved puzzle-platformers because they [b]force you to engage with a space[/b], not just run through it.
You’re not just a player with a gun or a quest marker — you’re an active participant, testing and understanding the environment.[/p][p]Games like [b]Portal[/b] and [b]Q.U.B.E. 2[/b] were huge inspirations.
Not just for their puzzle design, but for how they told story through environment, voice, and pacing.[/p][p]There’s something special about [b]solving a problem with your own reasoning[/b], not just following instructions.
It creates a personal connection between the player and the world.[/p][p]And from a design perspective:
We love how puzzle mechanics let us blend gameplay and narrative — making each room, each space, each object… [b]part of the story[/b].[/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45507777/3c7993b54d1e137f3a80c1494841dc68c5cf07b8.png"][/img][/p][h3]Why Thriller?[/h3][p][/p][p]Let’s be honest — nothing pulls you into a narrative like [b]tension and mystery[/b].
A sci-fi setting filled with clean corridors and logical puzzles is one thing…
But when you start to sense that something is [i]off[/i], that the place you’re in has a darker history… [b]that’s when immersion really kicks in[/b].[/p][p]Thrillers thrive on uncertainty. On half-answers. On making you question your next step.[/p][p]Our goal isn’t jumpscares or cheap shocks.
It’s that slow-building, creeping realization that maybe you’re not just solving puzzles…
Maybe you’re uncovering something you weren’t meant to find.[/p][p]And as the story unfolds across the chapters, the tone will shift — gradually, but noticeably.
What starts as clean and sterile will become more surreal… and more unsettling.[/p][p][/p][h3]Why Science?[/h3][p][/p][p]A more personal note here:
Many of us on the team have a genuine love for [b]science, math, and problem solving[/b].
And it felt natural to build a game where those things weren’t just “hidden under the hood” — but part of the experience.[/p][p]When we design puzzles, we think in logic gates, spatial constraints, cause and effect.
The kinds of things that engineers, mathematicians, and even philosophers grapple with in the real world.[/p][p]In many ways, [i]Project Enceladus[/i] is our way of celebrating how elegant problem-solving can feel… even in the middle of a narrative about psychological breakdown and ethical collapse.[/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45507777/0ac6534361f449b93b2be15d920752a2bbbeefed.png"][/img][/p][h3]And Finally… Why This Tone?[/h3][p][/p][p]Because for us, [b]the most memorable stories are the ones that leave a mark[/b].
That linger in your head after the credits roll.
That make you question the choices you made.[/p][p]We didn’t want to build a world that was "just another puzzle game"…
We wanted one that felt lived-in, broken, beautiful… and dangerous in ways that don’t rely on combat.[/p][p]A story that feels [b]personal, emotional, and human[/b] — even while set light-years away from home.[/p][p]Thanks for following our journey.
We can’t wait to show you more.[/p][p][/p][p][b]– The Dev Team[/b]
[/p]

notes.title: Meet the Team
notes.content:
[p]We’ve been sharing updates on the game itself — but not much about the people building it yet. So here’s a proper introduction to the small team behind Project Enceladus!  [/p][p][/p][h2]Where it all began...[/h2][p][/p][p]Before we ever opened Unreal Engine, or built puzzles, or placed a single light in the hangar —
[b]Project Enceladus began years ago as a world inside my head. [/b][/p][p][/p][p]I’ve always loved sci-fi and games. And over time, I started imagining a place — part memory, part story, part simulation.[/p][p]
At different times, I wanted to turn it into a novel, or run it as a roleplaying world with friends.
But the vision kept evolving — slowly, quietly — until I finally had the tools to bring it to life as a game.[/p][p][/p][p]This project started as a deeply personal challenge:[/p][list][*][p]To build something from scratch.[/p][/*][*][p]To give shape to the world I had in my head.[/p][/*][*][p]To learn, create, and tell a story through puzzles, mood, and space.[/p][/*][/list][p][/p][p]Today, that world is becoming real — and it’s called [b]Project Enceladus.[/b][/p][p][/p][p][b]– Tomi[/b][/p][p][/p][h2]Tomi – Coding, Game Design, Direction, Music & SFX, and everything in between[/h2][p]Tomi is an experienced C++ developer with a background in Unreal Engine, and the original one-man band behind the project.[/p][p]He’s worked on R&D projects using Unreal and C++, and developing a game became a creative breakout from the everyday technical grind — a space to experiment, tell stories, and build something personal.[/p][p][/p][p]He began with a clear goal: to build something from scratch, learn every part of the process, and grow through doing — from code and tech to art, music, and marketing.[/p][p][/p][p]You’ve probably noticed our team doesn’t really have a studio name — that’s because it wasn’t planned as a team project. But after a year of hard work, the game started gaining unexpected attention, and the solo effort quietly evolved into a passionate indie collaboration.
[/p][h2]Guci Dávid – 3D Generalist, Cinematic Motion & Visual Aesthetics[/h2][p]A 3D generalist with a background in cinematic motion work, Guci first helped out occasionally — jumping in when Tomi needed support with custom models or design tasks.[/p][p]Comfortable in both Blender and Unreal, and with a strong eye for mood and visual effect, he quickly became more than just an extra hand.
[/p][p]Guci was the first addition to the team — bringing style, structure, and visual depth to the project when it needed it most.[/p][p][/p][h2]FZoli – A Bit of Level Design, Support, Testing & Communication[/h2][p]The latest addition to the core team, Zoli started out as one of the many friends and coworkers who playtested early builds — spotting bugs, sharing thoughts, and brainstorming ideas with Tomi.
[/p][p]One thing led to another, and that casual feedback turned into deeper collaboration. Today, Zoli helps with level design, contributes ideas and direction, and supports the project through testing, posts, and web content.[/p][p]While still learning Unreal, he’s an experienced Unity developer with a strong background in game design, graphics, and shader programming — universal skills that come in handy on this Unreal project from time to time.
[/p][h2]And a Thank You[/h2][p]While this is the core team, we’ve been lucky to have many others support the project along the way — from friends and fellow developers who joined early playtests, to those who shared ideas, gave feedback, or just cheered us on.[/p][p]Your input has helped shape Project Enceladus more than you might think — so thanks for being part of the ride.[/p][p][/p][h2]Why We’re Making This[/h2][p]We’re a small team with a shared goal — one we didn’t even realize at first: we all just love puzzle games.[/p][p][/p][p]We’ve always admired games that tell stories through gameplay, where tone and design work hand in hand. Titles like Portal were early inspirations — not just for their puzzles, but for how they balanced atmosphere, pacing, and interaction.
[/p][p]Our aim is to create something that feels quiet through its puzzles, but intense as the story unfolds — a thoughtful, immersive experience that leaves space for the player to lean in.[/p][p][/p][p]Right now, we’re deep into Chapter I development, building on the tone and systems shaped during the Prologue.[/p][p]Thanks for following our journey — more soon![/p][p]
[b]– The Dev Team[/b]
[/p]

notes.title: Defining the Tone, Expanding the World
notes.content:
What we now call “the right tone” didn’t come easy.

The early stages of development — especially building the Prologue — were both a design and technical challenge.
There was a constant tension: how much to explain, how much to leave unsaid, and how to guide players through strange environments without breaking immersion.

At that time, the project was a one-developer effort — and staying true to that vision took time and iteration. Since then, it’s grown into a core team of three, supported by a circle of fellow developers, friends, and industry professionals who’ve helped shape the experience into something far stronger.

Closed playtests gave clarity on what worked, what needed space, and what didn’t land. We’re genuinely proud of where it ended up — not because it’s perfect, but because it feels like the voice of the game.

[h2]A Modular Core[/h2]

From the very beginning, the game was built around a modular system — every mechanic, logic piece, and puzzle was designed to be reusable and flexible.

That meant a ton of upfront work: writing systems, building tools, reworking elements multiple times to keep things clean and decoupled. But now, reaching Chapter I, that effort is paying off.

Levels are coming together through a mostly no-code workflow, allowing more focus on what matters: mood, interaction, pacing, space.

[h2]Where We’re Going[/h2]

Chapter I is where things start to open up. The structures we’ve built are letting us take more risks — and explore deeper layers of the world (and the minds within it).
It still follows the tone we’ve locked in, but now with more space to stretch and surprise.

[h2]What’s New[/h2]

We’ve recently added a bunch of new tools and features that are already transforming how we build and refine the game.

Our asset library has expanded significantly — and we’re now using procedural content generation (PCG) systems to speed up level creation without sacrificing detail or coherence.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45507777/f725ec4ec4aa4b6ea0bf73f7da89fe47dcc56d5c.png[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45507777/c5a3d22eb457541bcd67787ca625b329c654a387.png[/img]

Two major mechanics have also been added:
[list]
[*] A remote camera system, letting players interact with puzzles from a distance by viewing and activating elements through camera feeds.
[*] An energy switcher, which controls which puzzle branches are active at any given time — adding a new layer of strategic thinking to progression.
[/list]
We’ve also introduced logic gates into the puzzle systems, including basic conditions and more complex setups like XOR gates, giving us more control over how and when elements activate — and giving players more satisfying “aha!” moments.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45507777/09ef6521bfeb62221f31ce90045faaa1cb8b382b.png[/img]

Many of the in-game models have also been upgraded, bringing a richer level of visual polish that retroactively enhances earlier parts of the game and deepens overall immersion.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45507777/1f7ce7c019861ea06b5c4f138e0cd54208052be2.png[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45507777/6b2aeaaeed58e2a081aab081bb86235c23cdeaf4.png[/img]

And behind the scenes, Chapter I is progressing fast — with all these pieces helping it come together more efficiently than ever.

Besides, we finally have a [b]website[/b]! You can check it [url=https://projectenceladus.com/]here[/url].

Thanks for being here.

[b]– The Dev Team[/b]

notes.title: Looking Back: Pivots, Polish, and a MegaGrant Submission
notes.content:
While polishing the [b]Prologue levels[/b] and setting up our Steam page, we were also working toward something a bit bigger behind the scenes — we submitted the game for an [b]Epic MegaGrant[/b].

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45507777/26e93bcb29434fad3027dcc49750ebf6f4fede5e.png[/img]

It was an intense and exciting stretch of development. Now that we’ve caught our breath, we wanted to [b]look back and share a few things[/b] we haven’t talked about yet.

[h2]Playtests, Redesigns, and Late Shifts[/h2]

During internal playtests of the Prologue, we made some [b]last-minute redesigns[/b] that had a surprisingly big impact.

Some level elements were restructured, certain puzzles were fine-tuned, and in a few cases, entire areas were created for better pacing and clarity.
We’ve put together a few [b]before-and-after shots[/b] to show how things evolved.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45507777/bd313baa5ba1ae843a32d0ee442de43cb2f97eb4.png[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45507777/2f5d19a9c3555b47ca76e462dea5d5b5f81bf800.png[/img]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45507777/bc9d7d55dabdca02348cfdcdbbd02aa354bd2a9f.png[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45507777/e29f6bf585e016d778a0ca268fc1ad8ff590cebc.png[/img]

[h2]Quiet but Crucial Changes[/h2]

Beyond level design, we also made foundational improvements:
[list]
[*] We [b]rewrote the quality settings system[/b] to ensure the game’s mood and visual atmosphere stay intact — even on lower-end hardware.
[*] The [b]save system[/b] was fully implemented, including UI, slot management, and auto-saving.
[/list]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45507777/236fc2032b113ea2afc8b1c60f023d3ecc2f230d.png[/img]

[list]
[*] We added a Hint Log menu, so players can revisit important messages if they miss them.
[/list]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45507777/c3baef5b8d2ef4295115b02d177a9ceefd56d13d.png[/img]

[h2]Progress on Chapter I[/h2]

Development on Chapter I is in full swing. We’re building on everything we learned from the Prologue — designing new mechanics, refining how story and gameplay interact, and exploring more layered, mind-bending moments.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45507777/5103d39624a6b595d8f3b77376943fcbf3f64ee7.png[/img]

[url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5oI9JJbSaVc&ab_channel=ProjectEnceladus](You can catch a glimpse of this in our latest Devlog on YouTube.)[/url]

If you’re curious about what comes next, or just want to support the ride, [b]adding the game to your Wishlist really helps.[/b]

Thanks for being here.

[b]– The Dev Team[/b]

notes.title: 🎉 The Prologue is Complete – Development of Chapter I Has Begun!
notes.content:
We have exciting news to share: the final version of the Prologue is now complete! This is a huge milestone in development, and we’re thrilled to bring you this update.

Now that the Prologue is finished, we have shifted our focus entirely to developing Chapter I! In the coming weeks, we’ll be sharing sneak peeks of what we’re working on, and we can’t wait for you to see it.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45507777/34d601b55dbaaee2eb3d569611bc724b78758ab8.png[/img]

[b]What to expect in Chapter I?[/b]

[list]
[*] New gameplay mechanics
[*] Exciting story twists
[*] Deeper world-building and immersive experiences
[/list]

Stay tuned for more updates, and don’t forget to add the game to your wishlist! 🎮💙
